name: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
problem: Self-correction - asking a model to check and fix its own output - is widely assumed to improve reasoning without any external feedback or retraining.
mechanism: Not a mechanism but a CONTROL EXPERIMENT. Critically examines INTRINSIC self-correction, where the LLM attempts to correct its initial response based solely on its inherent capabilities, without external feedback, across model families, benchmarks, and prompt formulations.
speedup_reported: None, and that is the finding: LLMs struggle to self-correct without external feedback, and at TIMES PERFORMANCE EVEN DEGRADES after self-correction. Not recorded as a null but as the paper's negative result, which is load-bearing - it means self-correction loops are a pure COST with no expected accuracy return in the intrinsic setting. Any serving system implementing a self-correction retry loop is paying output tokens for tokens that measurably do not help.
notes: ADOPTION of the FINDING, not a technique: this paper is in production in the sense that its negative result shapes deployed designs - systems that ship self-correction retries do so with external verifiers or accept the cost knowingly. VENUE: ICLR 2024 per the arXiv comment field, so venue rests on the primary source. INCLUDED DELIBERATELY as the counterweight to the rest of the inference-time-compute sub-area: chain-of-thought, self-consistency, and budget forcing all spend output tokens expecting accuracy back, and this paper is the evidence that at least one common token-spending strategy does not deliver. The distinction it draws - intrinsic self-correction versus correction WITH EXTERNAL FEEDBACK - is the operative one, and a reader who quotes this as 'self-correction does not work' has over-read it; process supervision with a verifier (pap-eff-verify-step-by-step) is the external-feedback case that does work.
